opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think what I find most interesting is that failures are often far more revealing than successes. When you look at a beautiful generated image, it's easy to assume the model "understands" the scene: the lighting, the geometry, how objects relate to each other. But when you start pushing on it, asking for things like a specific number of objects, a reflection in a mirror that's actually consistent, text on a sign, or hands holding something in a physically plausible way, you start to see where that understanding is really just very good pattern matching.

Those failure modes tell you something about what the model has actually learned from the data versus what it's approximating. For example, if a model gets shadows mostly right but they don't agree with the light source when you look closely, that suggests it's learned the local statistics of what shadows look like without a coherent 3D model of the scene. That's useful to know, both scientifically and practically.

There's also a creative side to it. Coming from a background where I've worked on both graphics and vision, I like the detective work of designing prompts or inputs that isolate one specific capability, almost like building a controlled experiment. And then the payoff is that once you understand a failure systematically, rather than as a one-off funny artifact, you can measure it, track it across model versions, and hopefully feed that back into better training data or architectures.

And finally, as these models get deployed more widely, knowing where they break matters a lot. Users tend to trust outputs that look photorealistic, so understanding the subtle ways they go wrong is important for building tools people can actually rely on.

r001.rationale: The response discusses failures such as object counts, reflections, text, hands, and shadows, but does not mention full wine glasses or attribute difficulty to the prevalence of less-than-full examples.

r002.rationale: The response describes designing prompts as controlled experiments, but does not say that probing can be distributed across many people.

fable-5.1.text:
What I find fascinating is that the failures tell you so much more about what the model actually learned than the successes do. When a model produces a beautiful image, it's hard to know whether it understood the prompt or just landed on something plausible from the training distribution. But when it fails, you get a window into the shortcuts it's taking. Ask for a glass of wine filled to the brim and you get it half full, because that's what nearly every photo of wine looks like. Ask for a clock showing a specific time and you get ten past ten, because that's how watches are photographed in advertisements. Those aren't random bugs. They're the model revealing that it learned correlations in the visual world rather than the underlying concepts.

The other thing I like about it is that it's a very hands-on, almost playful kind of research. You poke at the model, you form a hypothesis about why it broke, and then you design a prompt to test that hypothesis. It feels closer to experimental psychology than to traditional benchmarking. Standard metrics tend to saturate quickly and they average over everything, so they hide exactly the interesting cases. Probing lets you find the sharp edges, the places where the model is confidently wrong, and those tend to be the most informative for figuring out what to fix next.

And honestly, those edges move fast. Things that were reliable failures a year ago, like hands or text rendering, are largely solved now, so the fun part is finding the next layer of failures that sits underneath, things like compositional reasoning, counting, spatial relationships, or physical plausibility. Each layer you peel back tells you something about where the capability actually comes from.

r001.rationale: The response says a request for a brim-full wine glass produces one that is half full because nearly every wine photo shows that pattern.

r002.rationale: It describes probing as hands-on and playful research, but does not say this work can be distributed across many people.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting is that these models can produce images that look incredibly convincing, but that doesn’t necessarily mean they’ve captured all the structure of what you’re asking for. An image can look great at first glance, and then you realize that a relationship between objects is wrong, or that some part of the prompt hasn’t been satisfied.

So probing those failures is a way of asking, what has the model actually learned? Can it combine familiar concepts in an unfamiliar way? Can it maintain consistency when you change one detail? I think those questions are useful both for understanding the models and for figuring out how to make them more useful. A beautiful output tells you what’s possible; understanding the failures helps you figure out when you can rely on it.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find interesting is that the failures can tell us something about how these models represent the world. You can generate an image that looks incredibly convincing at first glance, but then ask for a particular spatial relationship or a specific number of objects, and things start to break down. There’s this gap between producing something that looks plausible and actually satisfying all the constraints in a prompt.

So probing those failures becomes a way of asking, what has the model learned, and where does that understanding stop? And ideally, you’re finding systematic patterns, rather than just collecting funny examples. Those patterns give you something concrete to measure and, eventually, improve.
